subject: math
title: Grade 4 Area of Rectangles
seo_title: Grade 4 Area of Rectangles Worksheets: Free Math with Answer Key (Ontario Curriculum)
standard_text: Use the row and column structure of an array to measure the areas of rectangles and to show that the area of any rectangle can be found by multiplying its side lengths
meta_desc: Free Grade 4 area of rectangles worksheets for the Ontario math curriculum (E2.5, E2.6): count squares in rows and columns, use area = length × width in cm² and m², find a missing side, tell area from perimeter, and solve garden and rink problems. 100 questions with an answer key.
key_big: Area of a rectangle = length × width.
key_sub: The squares sit in equal rows, so multiply instead of counting. Missing side = area ÷ known side. Area is in cm² or m²; perimeter is in cm or m.
body_html:
Rows and columns of squares

Area is the number of unit squares that cover a shape. In a rectangle, the squares sit in equal rows. So you do not need to count them one by one: multiply.

You only need one row and one column to know how many squares fit.

Area = length × width

The length tells how many squares are in each row. The width tells how many rows there are. So area = length × width. Area is written in square units: cm² for small things, m² for big spaces like a floor, a garden or a rink.

Example

A rectangle is 14 m long and 5 m wide. What is its area?

14 × 5: 10 × 5 = 50 and 4 × 5 = 20. 50 + 20 = 70.

Answer: 70 m²

Find a missing side

If you know the area and one side, ask: what times this side gives the area? Divide: missing side = area ÷ known side.

Area or perimeter?

Area is the space inside (cm², m²). Perimeter is the distance around the edge (cm, m). Carpet, paint and tiles need the area. A fence, a border or rink boards need the perimeter.

Rectangle 8 cm by 5 cmHowAnswer
Area8 × 540 cm²
Perimeter8 + 5 + 8 + 526 cm

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Adding the sides (8 + 5 = 13)Multiply: 8 × 5 = 40 cm²
Finding the perimeter (8 + 5 + 8 + 5 = 26)That is the distance around. Area is the space inside
Writing cm or m for an areaArea is in square units: cm² or m²
Subtracting to find a missing side (48 − 8 = 40)Divide: 48 ÷ 8 = 6
Counting only the squares you can seeUse rows × squares in each row

faq.q: What do Grade 4 students learn about area in the Ontario math curriculum?
faq.a: They use the rows and columns of unit squares in a rectangle to see that area = length × width, find areas in cm² and m², and work out a missing side length when they know the area.

faq.q: How do you explain area = length × width to a child?
faq.a: Cover the rectangle with 1 cm squares. The squares make equal rows, so the number of rows times the squares in each row gives the area, which is width × length.

faq.q: How do you find a missing side if you know the area?
faq.a: Divide the area by the side you know. For example, a rectangle with an area of 48 m² and a length of 8 m is 48 ÷ 8 = 6 m wide.

faq.q: What is the difference between area and perimeter?
faq.a: Area is the space inside a shape, measured in square units such as cm² or m². Perimeter is the distance around the outside, measured in cm or m.

sets.title: Count squares in rows and columns

items.q: Only the top row and the left column of squares are drawn. How many squares would cover the whole rectangle?
items.e: The top row shows 9 squares in each row. The left column shows 4 rows. 4 × 9 = 36 squares.

items.q: A rectangle is covered by 3 rows of 1 cm² squares. There are 9 squares in each row. What is its area?
items.e: 3 rows of 9 squares: 3 × 9 = 27 squares, so the area is 27 cm².

items.q: Each square is 1 cm². What is the area of the shaded rectangle?
items.e: There are 3 rows with 7 squares in each row: 3 × 7 = 21. The area is 21 cm². (20 is the distance around the edge, the perimeter.)

items.q: What is the area of the shaded rectangle in square units?
items.e: There are 3 rows with 5 squares in each row: 3 × 5 = 15. The area is 15 square units. (16 is the distance around the edge, the perimeter.)

items.q: Each square is 1 cm². What is the area of the shaded rectangle?
items.e: There are 4 rows with 8 squares in each row: 4 × 8 = 32. The area is 32 cm². (24 is the distance around the edge, the perimeter.)

items.q: Kai counts the squares in a rectangle one by one: 5 rows of 8 squares, 40 in all. Which faster way gives the same answer?
items.e: 5 rows of 8 squares: 5 × 8 = 40. (5 + 8 = 13 adds a row and a column. 2 × 5 + 2 × 8 = 26 is the perimeter.)

items.q: What is the area of the shaded rectangle in square units?
items.e: There are 4 rows with 6 squares in each row: 4 × 6 = 24. The area is 24 square units. (20 is the distance around the edge, the perimeter.)

items.q: Each square is 1 cm². What is the area of the shaded rectangle?
items.e: There are 5 rows with 6 squares in each row: 5 × 6 = 30. The area is 30 cm². (22 is the distance around the edge, the perimeter.)

items.q: Which multiplication gives the number of squares in this rectangle?
items.e: There are 4 rows of 7 squares. 4 × 7 = 28 squares.

items.q: Only the top row and the left column of squares are drawn. How many squares would cover the whole rectangle?
items.e: The top row shows 8 squares in each row. The left column shows 5 rows. 5 × 8 = 40 squares.

items.q: Rectangle A has 3 rows of 8 squares. Rectangle B has 8 rows of 3 squares. Which is true?
items.e: 3 × 8 = 24 and 8 × 3 = 24. Turning a rectangle does not change its area.

items.e: There are 3 rows of 8 squares. 3 × 8 = 24 squares.

items.q: Which multiplication gives the number of squares in this rectangle?

items.e: 4 rows of 7 squares: 4 × 7 = 28 squares, so the area is 28 cm².

items.q: Which multiplication gives the number of squares in this rectangle?

items.q: Why can you multiply to find the number of squares in a rectangle?
c: Every row has the same number
The rows get longer and longer
items.e: In a rectangle, the squares sit in equal rows. Equal groups can be multiplied: number of rows × squares in each row.

items.q: What is the area of the shaded rectangle in square units?
items.e: There are 3 rows with 9 squares in each row: 3 × 9 = 27. The area is 27 square units. (24 is the distance around the edge, the perimeter.)

items.q: A rectangle is covered by 6 rows of 1 m² squares. There are 8 squares in each row. What is its area?
items.e: 6 rows of 8 squares: 6 × 8 = 48 squares, so the area is 48 m².

items.q: What is the area of this rectangle?
items.e: Area = length × width: 9 × 4 = 36 m². (26 m is the perimeter.)

items.q: A rectangle is 25 m long and 3 m wide. What is its area?
items.e: Area = length × width: 25 × 3. Split 25 into 20 + 5: 20 × 3 = 60 and 5 × 3 = 15. 60 + 15 = 75 m².

items.q: What is the area of this rectangle?
items.e: Area = length × width: 8 × 5 = 40 cm². (26 cm is the perimeter.)

items.q: Which unit is best for measuring the area of a backyard skating rink?
items.e: A rink is big and area is the space inside, so use square metres. cm and m measure length; cm² and m² measure area.

items.q: What is the area of this rectangle?
items.e: Area = length × width: 11 × 4 = 44 m². (30 m is the perimeter.)

items.q: Which unit is best for measuring the area of a hockey card?
items.e: A hockey card is small and area is the space inside, so use square centimetres. cm and m measure length; cm² and m² measure area.

items.q: Rectangle A is 6 cm by 4 cm. Rectangle B is 8 cm by 3 cm. Which has the bigger area?
items.e: A: 6 × 4 = 24 cm². B: 8 × 3 = 24 cm². The areas are the same, even though the shapes look different.

items.q: Which rule gives the area of a rectangle?
items.e: Area counts the squares inside: rows × squares in each row, which is length × width. Adding all four sides gives the perimeter.

items.q: A rectangle is 16 cm long and 6 cm wide. What is its area?
items.e: Area = length × width: 16 × 6. Split 16 into 10 + 6: 10 × 6 = 60 and 6 × 6 = 36. 60 + 36 = 96 cm².

items.q: What is the area of this rectangle?
items.e: Area = length × width: 12 × 3 = 36 m². (30 m is the perimeter.)

items.q: A rectangle is 18 cm long and 7 cm wide. What is its area?
items.e: Area = length × width: 18 × 7. Split 18 into 10 + 8: 10 × 7 = 70 and 8 × 7 = 56. 70 + 56 = 126 cm².

items.q: What is the area of this rectangle?
items.e: Area = length × width: 10 × 7 = 70 cm². (34 cm is the perimeter.)

items.q: A rectangle is 14 cm long and 5 cm wide. What is its area?
items.e: Area = length × width: 14 × 5. Split 14 into 10 + 4: 10 × 5 = 50 and 4 × 5 = 20. 50 + 20 = 70 cm².

items.q: What is the area of this rectangle?
items.e: Area = length × width: 7 × 6 = 42 cm². (26 cm is the perimeter.)

items.q: A rectangle is 23 m long and 4 m wide. What is its area?
items.e: Area = length × width: 23 × 4. Split 23 into 20 + 3: 20 × 4 = 80 and 3 × 4 = 12. 80 + 12 = 92 m².

items.q: A square has sides of 11 m. What is its area?
items.e: The length and width of a square are the same: 11 × 11 = 121 m².

items.q: A rectangle is 32 m long and 2 m wide. What is its area?
items.e: Area = length × width: 32 × 2. Split 32 into 30 + 2: 30 × 2 = 60 and 2 × 2 = 4. 60 + 4 = 64 m².

items.q: Which unit is best for measuring the area of a classroom floor?
items.e: A floor is big and area is the space inside, so use square metres. cm and m measure length; cm² and m² measure area.

items.q: Rectangle A is 9 m by 5 m. Rectangle B is 7 m by 7 m. Which has the bigger area?
items.e: A: 9 × 5 = 45 m². B: 7 × 7 = 49 m². 49 − 45 = 4, so B is bigger by 4 m². (9 + 5 and 7 + 7 are both 14, but adding the sides does not give the area.)

items.q: This is a square. What is its area?
items.e: The length and width of a square are the same: 9 × 9 = 81 cm².

items.q: A square has an area of 64 m². How long is each side?
items.e: Side × side = 64. 8 × 8 = 64, so each side is 8 m. (64 ÷ 4 = 16 would be the side if 64 were the perimeter.)

items.q: What is the length of the side marked ?
items.e: Length × width = area, so think: 6 × ? = 54. 54 ÷ 6 = 9, so the side is 9 cm. Check: 6 × 9 = 54 cm².

items.q: What is the length of the side marked ?
items.e: Length × width = area, so think: 8 × ? = 48. 48 ÷ 8 = 6, so the side is 6 cm. Check: 8 × 6 = 48 cm².

items.q: A rectangle has an area of 72 cm². One side is 9 cm. How long is the other side?
items.e: Length × width = area, so think: 9 × ? = 72. 72 ÷ 9 = 8, so the side is 8 cm. Check: 9 × 8 = 72 cm².

items.q: A rectangle has an area of 24 cm². Which could be its side lengths?
items.e: Area = length × width: 6 × 4 = 24 cm². 12 + 12 and 20 + 4 add to 24 instead. 10 cm and 2 cm give a perimeter of 24 cm, not an area of 24 cm².

items.q: Amira covers a rectangle with 63 square tiles, with no gaps. There are 7 rows. How many tiles are in each row?
items.e: 7 rows × ? = 63. 63 ÷ 7 = 9 tiles in each row. Check: 7 × 9 = 63.

items.q: A rectangle has an area of 45 m². One side is 9 m. How long is the other side?
items.e: Length × width = area, so think: 9 × ? = 45. 45 ÷ 9 = 5, so the side is 5 m. Check: 9 × 5 = 45 m².

items.q: A square has an area of 100 cm². How long is each side?
items.e: Side × side = 100. 10 × 10 = 100, so each side is 10 cm. (100 ÷ 4 = 25 would be the side if 100 were the perimeter.)

items.q: A rectangle has an area of 60 m². One side is 10 m. How long is the other side?
items.e: Length × width = area, so think: 10 × ? = 60. 60 ÷ 10 = 6, so the side is 6 m. Check: 10 × 6 = 60 m².

items.q: A square has an area of 36 cm². How long is each side?
items.e: Side × side = 36. 6 × 6 = 36, so each side is 6 cm. (36 ÷ 4 = 9 would be the side if 36 were the perimeter.)

items.q: A rectangle has an area of 36 m². Which could be its side lengths?
items.e: 9 × 4 = 36 m². 30 + 6 and 18 + 18 add to 36 instead. 10 m and 8 m give a perimeter of 36 m.

items.q: What is the length of the side marked ?
items.e: Length × width = area, so think: 6 × ? = 24. 24 ÷ 6 = 4, so the side is 4 cm. Check: 6 × 4 = 24 cm².

items.q: Nathan covers a rectangle with 40 square tiles, with no gaps. There are 5 rows. How many tiles are in each row?
items.e: 5 rows × ? = 40. 40 ÷ 5 = 8 tiles in each row. Check: 5 × 8 = 40.

items.q: Sofia covers a rectangle with 42 square tiles, with no gaps. There are 6 rows. How many tiles are in each row?
items.e: 6 rows × ? = 42. 42 ÷ 6 = 7 tiles in each row. Check: 6 × 7 = 42.

items.q: What is the length of the side marked ?
items.e: Length × width = area, so think: 7 × ? = 35. 35 ÷ 7 = 5, so the side is 5 m. Check: 7 × 5 = 35 m².

items.q: A rectangle has an area of 42 cm². One side is 7 cm. How long is the other side?
items.e: Length × width = area, so think: 7 × ? = 42. 42 ÷ 7 = 6, so the side is 6 cm. Check: 7 × 6 = 42 cm².

items.q: A rectangle has an area of 84 m². One side is 7 m. How long is the other side?
items.e: Length × width = area, so think: 7 × ? = 84. 84 ÷ 7 = 12, so the side is 12 m. Check: 7 × 12 = 84 m².

items.q: A rectangle has an area of 56 cm². One side is 8 cm. How long is the other side?
items.e: Length × width = area, so think: 8 × ? = 56. 56 ÷ 8 = 7, so the side is 7 cm. Check: 8 × 7 = 56 cm².

items.q: Each square is 1 cm by 1 cm. What are the area and the perimeter of the rectangle?
items.e: Area: 4 rows of 6 squares, 4 × 6 = 24 cm². Perimeter: 6 + 4 + 6 + 4 = 20 cm.

items.e: Area is the space inside: 9 × 5 = 45 cm². The perimeter would be 9 + 5 + 9 + 5 = 28 cm.

items.q: Ava wants to buy carpet to cover her bedroom floor. What should she find?
items.e: Carpet covers the space inside, so find the area. A floor is big, so use square metres.

items.q: A square has a perimeter of 20 cm. What is its area?
items.e: 4 equal sides make 20 cm, so each side is 20 ÷ 4 = 5 cm. Area = 5 × 5 = 25 cm². (400 uses 20 as the side.)

items.q: A rectangle has an area of 24 m² and a length of 8 m. What is its perimeter?
items.e: First find the width: 24 ÷ 8 = 3 m. Then the perimeter: 8 + 3 + 8 + 3 = 22 m. (11 m adds only one length and one width.)

items.q: Priya wants to cover the front of her notebook with stickers. What should she find?
items.e: Stickers cover the space inside, so find the area. A notebook is small, so use square centimetres.

items.q: What is the perimeter of this rectangle?
items.e: Perimeter is the distance around: 9 + 2 + 9 + 2 = 22 m. (9 × 2 = 18 m² is the area.)

items.q: Lucas wants to put a fence around his vegetable garden. What should he find?
items.e: A fence goes around the edge, so find the perimeter. It is a length, in metres.

items.q: Aiden wants to glue ribbon around the edge of his card. What should he find?
items.e: Ribbon goes around the edge, so find the perimeter. A card is small, so use centimetres.

items.q: Each square is 1 cm by 1 cm. What are the area and the perimeter of the rectangle?
items.e: Area: 3 rows of 5 squares, 3 × 5 = 15 cm². Perimeter: 5 + 3 + 5 + 3 = 16 cm.

items.q: Which rectangle has an area of 16 m² and a perimeter of 16 m?
items.e: 4 × 4 = 16 m² and 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 = 16 m. (8 by 2 has a perimeter of 20 m; 6 by 2 and 5 by 3 have areas of 12 m² and 15 m².)

items.q: Both rectangles have an area of 24 cm²: one is 6 cm by 4 cm, the other is 8 cm by 3 cm. Which has the longer perimeter?
items.e: 6 cm by 4 cm: 6 + 4 + 6 + 4 = 20 cm. 8 cm by 3 cm: 8 + 3 + 8 + 3 = 22 cm. The same area can have different perimeters.

items.q: What is the area of this rectangle?
items.e: Area is the space inside: 7 × 4 = 28 cm². The perimeter would be 7 + 4 + 7 + 4 = 22 cm.

items.q: What is the area of this rectangle?
items.e: Area is the space inside: 8 × 7 = 56 cm². The perimeter would be 8 + 7 + 8 + 7 = 30 cm.

items.q: Which rectangle has an area of 12 cm² and a perimeter of 14 cm?
items.e: 4 × 3 = 12 cm² and 4 + 3 + 4 + 3 = 14 cm. (6 by 2 has a perimeter of 16 cm; 5 by 2 has an area of 10 cm².)

items.q: What is the perimeter of this rectangle?
items.e: Perimeter is the distance around: 6 + 2 + 6 + 2 = 16 m. (6 × 2 = 12 m² is the area.)

items.q: What is the perimeter of this rectangle?
items.e: Perimeter is the distance around: 8 + 3 + 8 + 3 = 22 m. (8 × 3 = 24 m² is the area.)

items.q: What is the area of this rectangle?
items.e: Area is the space inside: 10 × 4 = 40 cm². The perimeter would be 10 + 4 + 10 + 4 = 28 cm.

items.q: What is the perimeter of this rectangle?
items.e: Perimeter is the distance around: 12 + 5 + 12 + 5 = 34 m. (12 × 5 = 60 m² is the area.)

items.q: Both rectangles have a perimeter of 20 m: one is 6 m by 4 m, the other is 9 m by 1 m. Which has the bigger area?
items.e: 6 × 4 = 24 m² and 9 × 1 = 9 m². The same perimeter can give very different areas.

sets.title: Word problems: gardens, rinks and floors

items.q: The reading corner is 5 m long and 3 m wide. Each carpet tile covers 1 m². How many tiles cover it?
items.e: 3 rows of 5 tiles: 3 × 5 = 15 tiles. (5 + 3 = 8 adds the sides, and 16 m is the perimeter.)

items.q: Ethan’s garden has an area of 32 m². It is 8 m long. How wide is it?
items.e: 8 × ? = 32. 32 ÷ 8 = 4, so the garden is 4 m wide. (24 comes from subtracting: 32 − 8.)

items.q: Mateo makes a bookmark 18 cm long and 5 cm wide. What is its area?
items.e: 18 × 5: 10 × 5 = 50 and 8 × 5 = 40, so 50 + 40 = 90 cm². (58 comes from 10 × 5 + 8, forgetting to multiply the 8.)

items.q: Jayden’s family floods a backyard rink that is 12 m long and 7 m wide. What is the area of the ice?
items.e: Area = length × width: 12 × 7 = 84 m². (12 + 7 + 12 + 7 = 38 m is the distance around.)

items.q: Hana makes a poster for the Terry Fox Run. It is 50 cm long and 30 cm wide. What is its area?
items.e: 50 × 30: 5 × 3 = 15, then add the two zeros: 1500 cm². (160 cm is the perimeter; 80 adds the sides.)

items.q: A quilt is made of squares in 8 rows with 7 squares in each row. How many squares are in the quilt?
items.e: 8 rows of 7: 8 × 7 = 56 squares. (26 counts only the squares around the edge.)

items.q: The school has two sandboxes. Each one is 3 m long and 2 m wide. What is the total area of the sandboxes?
items.e: One sandbox: 3 × 2 = 6 m². Two sandboxes: 6 + 6 = 12 m². (10 m is the perimeter of one sandbox.)

items.q: A backyard rink is 12 m long and 7 m wide. Boards go all the way around it. How many metres of boards are needed?
items.e: Boards go around the edge, so find the perimeter: 12 + 7 + 12 + 7 = 38 m. (31 m leaves out one side.)

items.q: Emma’s garden is 7 m by 5 m. Arjun’s garden is 6 m by 6 m. Whose garden has the bigger area?
items.e: Emma: 7 × 5 = 35 m². Arjun: 6 × 6 = 36 m². 36 − 35 = 1, so Arjun’s garden is bigger by 1 m². (7 + 5 and 6 + 6 are both 12, but adding the sides does not give the area.)

items.q: The teacher has 30 carpet tiles. The circle-time carpet needs 4 rows of 6 tiles. How many tiles are left over?
items.e: Carpet: 4 × 6 = 24 tiles. Left over: 30 − 24 = 6 tiles. (20 comes from 30 − 4 − 6.)

items.q: Each gym mat is 2 m long and 1 m wide. The class lays 9 mats on the floor with no gaps or overlaps. What area do the mats cover?
items.e: One mat: 2 × 1 = 2 m². 9 mats: 9 × 2 = 18 m². (27 comes from 9 × 3, adding 2 + 1 first.)

items.q: Liam covers a table 9 tiles long and 6 tiles wide with square tiles. He has put down 30 tiles. How many more tiles does he need?
items.e: Whole table: 9 × 6 = 54 tiles. Still needed: 54 − 30 = 24 tiles.

items.q: On a snow day, the class marks out a snow fort 5 m long and 5 m wide. What is its area?
items.e: 5 × 5 = 25 m². (20 m is the distance around, and area is in m², not m.)

items.q: Mei’s bedroom floor is 4 m by 3 m. A rug 2 m by 2 m lies on it. What area of floor is not covered?
items.e: Floor: 4 × 3 = 12 m². Rug: 2 × 2 = 4 m². 12 − 4 = 8 m². (2 m² comes from (4 − 2) × (3 − 2), which takes away from the sides instead of the areas.)

items.q: A rectangular garden has an area of 40 m². It is 5 m wide. How much fence goes all the way around it?
items.e: Length: 40 ÷ 5 = 8 m. Fence: 8 + 5 + 8 + 5 = 26 m. (13 m adds only one length and one width; 18 m adds the width twice and the length once.)

items.q: Owen’s class plants a vegetable garden 6 m long and 4 m wide. What is the area of the garden?
items.e: 6 × 4 = 24 m². (6 + 4 = 10 adds the sides, and 20 m is the perimeter.)

items.q: A classroom floor is 9 m long and 8 m wide. What is its area?
items.e: 9 × 8 = 72 m². Area is in square metres. (34 m is the perimeter.)

items.q: A garden is 6 m long and 4 m wide. How much fence goes all the way around it?
items.e: A fence goes around the edge: 6 + 4 + 6 + 4 = 20 m. (24 m² is the area.)

items.q: Leah paints a garage wall that is 5 m long and 3 m high. One can of paint covers 5 m². How many cans does she need?
items.e: Area of the wall: 5 × 3 = 15 m². Each can covers 5 m²: 15 ÷ 5 = 3 cans.

items.q: A banner for Canada Day is 4 m long and 1 m wide. What area of cloth is needed to make it?
items.e: 4 × 1 = 4 m². (10 m is the distance around the banner, and 4 + 1 = 5 adds the sides.)
